CHRISTIAN COOMER.name: Christian Coomer
CHRISTIAN COOMER.background: Republican. Cartersville attorney with his own law practice; judge advocate in the U.S. Air Force Reserve JAG Corps. Bachelor's degree, Lee University; J.D., University of Georgia. Represented Georgia House District 14 from 2011 to 2018 (won a 2010 primary runoff over Shep Helton by 51.4%; unopposed 2012-2018) and was House majority whip in 2018. Gov. Nathan Deal appointed him to the Georgia Court of Appeals on Sept. 14, 2018 (took office Oct. 31, 2018); elected unopposed to the court in 2020. Removed from the bench by the Georgia Supreme Court on Aug. 16, 2023; succeeded by J. Wade Padgett.
CHRISTIAN COOMER.record: In the House he served on Banks and Banking, Ethics, Judiciary (Non-Civil), Juvenile Justice, Retirement (vice chair), Rules and Transportation at various times, and was majority whip in 2018. As a judge: in March 2020 the Judicial Qualifications Commission opened an inquiry after a former client (Jim Filhart) sued him alleging fraud and legal malpractice; Coomer said, "I completely and utterly deny the allegations of fraud," and the GBI also investigated. He repaid the loans and settled the suit in July 2020 on confidential terms. The JQC filed ethics charges in late December 2020, and the Supreme Court suspended him with pay on Jan. 5, 2021. In December 2021 he agreed to a $25,000 fine with the state ethics commission, which said he moved money from his House campaign account to his law firm as short-term loans in 2015-2019 and failed to disclose expenditures; commission staff called it the largest ethics fine ever assessed against a Georgia judge. The Supreme Court upheld his removal from office on Aug. 16, 2023. The unanimous Aug. 16, 2023 Supreme Court ruling (49 pages) upheld a JQC hearing panel's findings: he accepted several loans from elderly client James Filhart, including an unsecured $130,000 loan in 2018 to a business he controlled with no assets (repaid in 2020 after Filhart sued); drafted a will for Filhart naming Coomer and his heirs as beneficiaries and Coomer as executor and trustee; moved campaign funds to his law firm's account without reporting some transfers; and billed a leisure trip to Hawaii as legislative business (later reimbursed).
